title: The maturity phases of running evals — Phil Hetzel, Braintrust

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

The evaluation methodology applies broadly to agent quality across any application vertical rather than a specific domain. The eval flywheel explicitly spans pre-production eval design, production trace capture, and offline experimentation for iterative improvement. summary: Phil Hetzel, who leads solutions engineering at Braintrust, outlines the maturity levels teams traverse as they build evals for AI agents. He frames evals as fundamentally different from unit tests: unit tests are exhaustive, while evals should target known failure modes identified by builders or subject matter experts. Trying to cover every possible failure is infinite and unproductive. Evals serve agent quality defensively, mitigating reputational, cost, compliance, and legal risks, and offensively, measuring improvement with each tweak. Three primitives define every eval: a task, a dataset of initiating examples, and scoring functions. The first maturity stage is vibe checking, which Hetzel defends as a valid starting point, provided human annotators document not just thumbs up or down but written justifications. These justifications capture domain-specific knowledge that can later be scaled. The second stage expands by deriving failure modes from those justifications and automating evaluation via LLM-as-judge or deterministic code checks, while cautioning that LLM judges must themselves be evaluated. The third stage addresses tool calls that interact with external systems, split into context gathering tools and CRUD-based tools. Context gathering tools merely inject data into the LLM, but CRUD tools create, read, update, or delete information, requiring evaluation of the entire agent trace rather than just the output. Two hard problems emerge: representing the state of external systems at the time the eval input was created, and interacting with those systems without overwriting production data. Two approaches are presented: injecting captured system state directly into the arbitrarily large trace itself, and performing timestamp or version queries against systems such as vector databases that support them. These are emerging, more complex techniques. Looking ahead, Hetzel points to topic modeling at scale to automatically uncover failure modes in production and automated eval workflows using cloud code and eval provider CLIs. In Q&A, he advocates embracing LLM-as-judge for subjective dimensions while evaluating the judge itself against ground truth, since LLM judge outputs are discrete and amenable to deterministic comparison. The overarching concept remains a flywheel: production traces reveal failures, which feed back into offline experimentation, which guides the next improvement.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Phil Hetzel introduces himself as lead of solutions engineering at Braintrust. He spent 12 years in consulting at KPMG and Slalom Consulting, where he noticed customers excelled at generative AI proofs of concept but struggled to bring them to production. He joined Braintrust after using it as a customer. He previews a talk on maturity levels of agent evals, focused on theory over product.

sections.title: What is Braintrust and why evals matter
sections.summary: Braintrust is an agent quality company contributing through evals and observability, treated as the same systems problem. Evals build confidence before production; observability maintains confidence in production. Evals defend against reputational, cost, and compliance risks, and also play offense by measuring improvement with each agent tweak.

sections.title: Eval primitives and contrast with unit tests
sections.summary: Hetzel states evals are not unit tests. Unit tests are exhaustive; evals should start high-level with known failure modes identified by builders or subject matter experts. Trying to cover every possible failure is infinite and unproductive. Eval results need not be perfect; directional trends from LLM-as-judge are acceptable. Every eval has three primitives: a task, a dataset of examples, and scoring functions.

sections.title: Maturity stage one: vibe checking with documentation
sections.summary: Stage one is vibe checking, which Hetzel defends as better than nothing. The key recommendation is to document: human annotators (ideally subject matter experts) should provide thumbs up or down plus a written justification for why. This extracts domain knowledge that can later be scaled into LLM-as-judge. Braintrust lets teams live-code custom annotation views tailored to their agent traces rather than using a generic interface.

sections.title: Maturity stage two: scaling human knowledge via LLM-as-judge and the flywheel
sections.summary: Stage two derives failure modes from human justifications and automates evaluation via LLM-as-judge or deterministic code checks (e.g., too many tool calls, too many tokens). Hetzel warns that LLM judges must be evaluated, not trusted blindly. Critically, eval datasets should capture production or UAT traces so evals approximate rerunning production. The flywheel concept: production traces surface failures, which feed into offline experimentation, guiding the next improvement. The section ends as Hetzel begins introducing complexity beyond simple model calls.

sections.title: Maturity stage three: tool calls, external systems, and emerging patterns
sections.summary: Hetzel distinguishes context gathering tools, which inject data into the LLM, from CRUD-based tools, which create, read, update, or delete information in external systems. CRUD tools force evaluation of the entire agent trace, not just the output, requiring tooling to capture and introspect large traces and target evals at individual tool or MCP calls. Two hard problems arise: representing external system state at the time the eval input was created, and interacting with those systems without overwriting production data. Two emerging approaches are injecting captured system state directly into the arbitrarily large trace, and performing timestamp or version queries against systems such as vector databases that support them. Hetzel also points to topic modeling at scale for auto-discovering failure modes and automated eval workflows using cloud code and eval provider CLIs. In Q&A he recommends embracing LLM-as-judge for subjective dimensions while evaluating the judge itself against ground truth, noting that discrete judge outputs make this feasible.

demonstrations: Braintrust human annotator view that lets teams live-code their own annotation interfaces tailored to their agent traces
limitations: Trying to write evals for every possible failure mode is infinite and leaves no time for shipping.
LLM-as-judge will not achieve 100% accuracy; results may be directional rather than perfect.
LLM judges are not inherently more trustworthy just because they are LLMs and should be evaluated themselves.
Representing external system state at the time an eval input was created is not completely solved.
Interacting with CRUD-based external systems during offline evals risks overwriting production data.
State injection and timestamp query techniques are emerging and more complex, not yet standard practice.

evidence.excerpt: Evals are not unit tests where whereas unit tests are very exhaustive in in how you perform them. With evals you want to make sure that you start very high-level with the failure modes of your agent.
evidence.supports: Evals differ from unit tests by focusing on known failure modes rather than exhaustive coverage.

evidence.excerpt: you should make that human annotator perform a justification for why they chose that thumbs up up or thumbs down.
evidence.supports: Stage one requires documented justifications alongside thumbs up or down judgments.

evidence.excerpt: we want to be able to capture these traces these agent traces in production, understand what's going wrong with them either through a human or or through automated tooling, and then bring those examples back to some offline experimentation environment
evidence.supports: The eval flywheel connects production traces to offline experimentation and improvement.

evidence.excerpt: just because you put a robe and a cloak on an LLM, that doesn't make it inherently more trustworthy. You should be evaluating LLMs as judge outputs as well.
evidence.supports: LLM judges must themselves be evaluated, not trusted blindly.

evidence.excerpt: I think of of tool calls in two different ways. There is context gathering tools that are just, uh, gathering data and injecting that into the LLM. And then there is CRUD-based tools where you're creating, reading, updating, or deleting information from a database or an external system.
evidence.supports: Tool calls split into context gathering tools and CRUD-based tools, both affecting agent quality and failure surface.

evidence.excerpt: really challenging to represent the state that the other external systems were were in at the time that eval input was created. And then two, it makes it really challenging to interact with those systems that the agent could be interacting with because you don't want to overwrite any production data.
evidence.supports: Two hard problems with CRUD tool evals: representing past external system state and avoiding production data corruption.

evidence.excerpt: if a trace can be arbitrarily large, you can actually cram in a ton of context, i.e. system state, the state that the external systems were in at the time, into these traces and inject that into a into the task that you're running the eval upon.
evidence.supports: Captured system state can be injected directly into traces to approximate the production environment during offline evals.

evidence.excerpt: you can run a version query to query the vector database at a certain point in time. So, that way you're adequately representing the state of of when that task ran originally.
evidence.supports: Timestamp or version queries against vector databases can represent system state at the time the original task ran.

evidence.excerpt: I would embrace LLM as judge, but also perform a lot of evals on the LLM as judge so that like it's it's very aligned with what a human would decide in the same circumstance. You would eval the eval as an eval.
evidence.supports: Embrace LLM-as-judge for subjective dimensions but evaluate the judge itself against human ground truth.
